schools.summary: Gill says it is not easy to say how these tribes came to have more cattle in proportion than the rest, and supposes they were more addicted to the pastoral life and more diligent in the care of their beasts; he cites Aben Ezra for the view that the Gadites were the authors of the counsel.

Henry rejects the supposition that they brought more cattle out of Egypt, on the ground that forty years is long enough for stocks to change, and prefers better husbandry; he draws from the whole transaction the principle that even when much was being done by extraordinary Providence, many things were left to human prudence, since God makes use of the reason of men.

Keil and Delitzsch explain the emphatic apposition in the first clause, place Gilead across two modern provinces north and south of the Jabbok, and note that ancient Gilead still shows traces of great fertility; Ellicott adds that the two tribes had encamped contiguously for thirty-eight years and would naturally wish to remain neighbours.
Wesley reduces the geography to a line, a city and country of the Amorites and a mountainous country famous for pasturage.

debates.question: Why had these two tribes so much more cattle than the rest?
debates.positions: Gill declines to settle it and guesses at a stronger inclination to the pastoral life; Henry reports and rejects the common supposition that they brought more out of Egypt, since that was forty years before and stocks of cattle increase and decrease in less time, and prefers better husbandry, that they had not been so profuse as their neighbours in eating the lambs out of the flock.

debates.question: Why is Gad named first after the opening verse?
debates.positions: Gill relays Aben Ezra that the Gadites were the authors of the counsel and moved it first to the Reubenites camped beside them; Henry offers that they were either the most forward or the better spokesmen, and adds a third consideration, that Reuben tribe still lay under the sentence that he should not excel.

outliers.view: Draws from the episode a rule about providence and prudence, that God in governing both the world and the church makes use of the reason of men and serves his own purposes by it, even in an age of extraordinary divine appearances.

themes: a very great multitude of cattle
the land of Jazer and the land of Gilead
a place for cattle
prudence inside providence
Reuben named first and Gad named after

schools.summary: Calvin condemns the request while allowing what can be allowed for it, that it was apparently reasonable and their modesty praiseworthy since they sought permission rather than seizing, yet holds that private interest had so mastered them that the main point escaped them, that their association for the war was established by God and the land of Canaan assigned to the whole race of Abraham; Gill notes that one of the towns is named nowhere else in Scripture.

Ellicott sets two readings of the request against each other and prefers the stronger, and closes with the long-range fact that these tribes were among the first carried into captivity by the king of Assyria; Keil and Delitzsch allow the milder reading on the strength of the men later declaration, and note that the clause about the country the Lord smote describes a land without a ruler.
Henry files the motives under two heads, the lust of the eye and the pride of life, the land being not only pleasant to look at but good for food.
Clarke summarises the chapter as a whole and identifies the towns as having belonged to Sihon and Og.

debates.question: What were the two tribes actually asking for?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch allow that the words about not crossing the Jordan may express nothing more than a wish about where their inheritance should lie, with no intention of withdrawing help, and point to the men subsequent declaration; Ellicott concedes that reading but prefers a stronger one, that the words may equally be taken, as Moses appears to have understood them and as they were in all probability designed to be understood, as a request that the conquest of the western side be left to the other tribes.

debates.question: How culpable was the request?
debates.positions: Calvin condemns it most heavily, as a severance from the body of the Church and a transgression of limits God had set, while granting that their modesty in asking rather than seizing was praiseworthy; Henry files it under the lust of the eye and the pride of life; Ellicott judges more coolly that the language indicated selfish consideration and was calculated to dishearten their brethren.

outliers.view: Takes the verb about seeing the land as a warning in itself, that we beware lest our eyes by unlawful looks lead us into snares and blind our minds, so that our senses are deceived by an envenomed sweetness.
Closes the account of the request with a fact from long afterwards, that these two tribes and the half tribe of Manasseh were among the first taken into captivity by the king of Assyria.

themes: let this land be given unto thy servants
bring us not over Jordan
the country which the LORD smote
a land without a ruler
the lust of the eye

schools.summary: Calvin ranks the two charges explicitly and puts ingratitude towards God above injustice towards their brethren, argues that the very severity of the reproof proves the greatness of the wrong rather than any warmth in Moses, and distinguishes the comparison Moses actually makes, not to the whole people but to the ten spies from whom the sedition arose; Gill counts the practical loss of two thirds of a standard as well as the moral one.

Henry names three faults together, disregard to the land of Canaan, distrust of the promise, and unwillingness to encounter danger, and turns the rebuke into a rule about not sitting down unconcerned at the perilous concerns of others.

Keil and Delitzsch order the charges as the speech orders them, want of brotherly feeling first and discouragement of the others second, and render the idiom literally as holding the heart away; Ellicott says the verb rendered discourage means rather to alienate or avert.
Wesley compresses the contrast into a line, that they would sit in ease and peace while their brethren were engaged in a bloody war.

debates.question: What is Moses chiefly rebuking?
debates.positions: Gill names covetousness and cowardice; Henry names disregard of Canaan, distrust of the promise and unwillingness to face danger; Keil and Delitzsch put want of brotherly feeling first and the discouraging of the other tribes second; Calvin ranks them and says explicitly that the ingratitude and perverseness towards God is chastised more severely than the injustice towards their brethren.

outliers.view: Defends the sharpness of the reproof as evidence rather than excess, that neither did inconsiderate warmth carry Moses into such anger nor did he pronounce on a matter he did not understand, since the two tribes desired to lacerate the body of the Church by this severance.

Distinguishes the comparison Moses makes, that he does not liken the Reubenites and Gadites to the whole rebellious people but specifically to the ten spies from whom the sedition arose, since so far as in them lay they turned the people aside from the right way.

themes: shall your brethren go to war and shall ye sit here
wherefore discourage ye the heart
thus did your fathers
the ten spies and not the whole people
holding the heart away

schools.summary: Gill takes the anger to have been kindled against the spies and against the people who murmured on their report, and argues at length that the epithet Kenezite belongs to the father rather than to Caleb, with reasons from the marriage of Othniel and from the constant naming of Jephunneh as the father; Calvin takes the word for what the sons are to their fathers as an addition or climax and names the renderings he rejects.

Clarke states flatly that it was Jephunneh who was the Kenezite and not Caleb, supposing Kenaz probably his father; Wesley takes the same descent one generation further back, from Kenaz his grandfather.

Ellicott notes that Moses is here declaring the fulfilment of the very prediction he himself announced when the evil report was brought up; Keil and Delitzsch render the threat plainly, that if these men draw back God will leave the nation still longer in the desert so that they prepare destruction for the whole people.
Henry draws the moral the passage is pointed at, that if men considered as they ought what would be the end of sin they would be afraid of the beginning of it.

debates.question: Who was the Kenezite, and how does the descent run?
debates.positions: Gill argues for the father rather than Caleb, since it will not suit to derive the name from the Kenaz who fathered Othniel, Othniel being called Caleb brother though Caleb gave him his daughter, and since Jephunneh and never Kenaz is named as Caleb father, concluding that both were named from a remoter ancestor and relaying a rabbinic reading that made Caleb rather the son-in-law of Kenaz; Clarke agrees the epithet is the father and supposes Kenaz his father; Wesley makes Kenaz the grandfather.

debates.question: How should the word for what the sons are to their fathers be rendered?
debates.positions: Calvin takes it as an addition and specifically a climax, holding that those translate poorly who render it education, or offspring, or foster-children, since the noun comes from a root meaning to increase and multiply and is applied for that reason to usury; the passage, he argues, requires the sense of a heap, a new body of persons springing up who carry impiety to its height.

outliers.view: Compares the doubling of guilt by imitation to a later preacher reproach that his hearers always resisted the Holy Ghost as their fathers did, and draws from the phrase about not fulfilling after the Lord that there is nothing praiseworthy in the most vigorous course unless men persevere even to the goal.

themes: the LORD anger was kindled
save Caleb the son of Jephunneh
forty years in the wilderness
risen up in your fathers stead
fuel added to a smouldering fire

schools.summary: Henry raises the question whether the two tribes had meant this all along and refuses to settle it, drawing a separate lesson from each branch, that honest meaning is often unhappily misinterpreted, or that plain dealing has a good effect.

Calvin settles it the second way and makes the severity of Moses the cause, since a milder dealing would perhaps have been received with contempt, and notes the one advantage the tribes still keep, the opportunity of improving their domestic finances while their families sit safe.

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both read the verb as rebuilding or repair rather than founding, and describe the folds as loose stones piled one upon another; Keil and Delitzsch add a traveller report that nomads still ring each camp with a stone enclosure whose falling top stones betray a wolf at night.
Clarke reaches the same conclusion from impossibility, that cities could not have been built and fortified in the time, and cites Calmet for repairing the Amorite cities lately taken.

debates.question: Had the two tribes intended to send their fighting men all along?
debates.positions: Henry poses the question and declines to answer it, drawing a lesson from either possibility, that what is honestly meant is often misinterpreted and Moses was excusable in suspecting the worst out of care to prevent sin, or that plain dealing brought them to their duty without murmuring; Calvin answers it, holding that the reply shows how usefully the severity of Moses had worked on their minds, since gentleness would have been received with contempt.

outliers.view: Support the description of the sheepfolds from a modern traveller account of nomads who ring each camping place with a stone wall the height of a man, so that the noise of the smaller stones laid on top betrays a wolf attempting to enter in the night.
Notes what the compromise still leaves the two tribes, that by depositing their wives and children in a peaceful spot they would have the opportunity of improving their domestic finances.

themes: we will build sheepfolds here for our cattle
cities for our little ones
repair rather than found
a stone wall the height of a man
the good effect of plain dealing

schools.summary: Clarke asks who was to defend the fortified cities if only women and children were left, denies it possible, and proves from the census figures against the number recorded as crossing that some seventy thousand men must have stayed behind; Wesley reads the promise as elastic from the outset, that they undertook to go either all or as many as should be thought necessary.

Ellicott renders the phrase as equipping themselves in haste, notes that the word for little ones seems to cover the whole defenceless portion of the nation, and treats the nineteenth verse as a critical passage bearing on a word applied to the country on both banks of the river; Keil and Delitzsch set out the promise in its parts.
Gill insists the disclaimer was not said in contempt of the good land nor as a refusal, but as giving up all pretensions to any share there if their own request were granted.

debates.question: Did every fighting man of the two tribes go over?
debates.positions: Clarke says it cannot be supposed possible that women and children could hold fortified cities, and counts the three tribal numbers from the last census against the forty thousand recorded as crossing armed, concluding that seventy thousand five hundred and eighty were left behind for the defence of the families; Wesley reads the undertaking as elastic from the start, either all or as many as should be thought necessary; Gill, on the terms Moses sets, notes that Moses is very express in requiring not some of them only but all.

debates.question: Does the phrase on this side Jordan fix where the writer stood?
debates.positions: Ellicott treats the verse as one of the critical passages bearing on the question and answers that it does not, since the same word is applied here to the country on both sides of the river, so that nothing can be inferred with any degree of certainty about whether the writer was east or west of it.

outliers.view: Settles a question of numbers by arithmetic rather than exposition, setting the census totals of the three tribes against the figure recorded as actually crossing the Jordan armed, and naming the peoples the defenders were left to guard against.

themes: we will go ready armed before the children of Israel
our little ones shall dwell in the fenced cities
we will not return unto our houses
on this side Jordan eastward
a promise larger than the muster

schools.summary: Ellicott infers from the phrase about going armed before the Lord that Israel army was regarded as the army of the Lord and that the ark was carried into war, supporting it from the order of march and two later scenes, and observes that the two tribes do not adopt the phrase until Moses has used it first.

Calvin raises an objection against Moses that no other witness raises, that he extended boundaries God had prescribed and gave an immediate answer without consulting God, and then answers it from the later history; on the closing warning he holds that vengeance is so connected with sin that it cannot be severed from it; Gill notes that Moses is very express, requiring a crossing and not a march, and all of them and not some.
Wesley reads the phrase of the ark as the token of God presence, and turns the warning about sin finding them out into a duty, that we should find our sins out first so as to repent of them.

debates.question: Did Moses exceed his commission in granting the request?
debates.positions: Calvin poses the objection in its full force, that the inheritance had been promised in Canaan and it was not allowable for Moses to alter a divine decree, and that in a matter of such perplexity he did not consult God but gave an immediate answer indirectly overthrowing the previous ordinance; he answers from the outcome, that God pardoned the error and took occasion to extend his liberality, and that the arrangement was ratified after Moses death and excepted in the later assignment of inheritances, from which it is evident his decision was approved. No other witness raises the question.

debates.question: What does going armed before the Lord mean?
debates.positions: Ellicott takes it of the ark carried into war and argues it from the order of march, in which these two tribes immediately preceded the ark; Wesley allows either the order of march or the manner of the passage over Jordan; Gill takes the passage as the reference, the ark going first into the river and standing there while the tribes went over.

outliers.view: Reads the saying that sin will find them out as stronger than a plain statement that they shall not escape, since it means that vengeance is so connected with sin that it cannot be severed from it, and warns that God forbearance encourages us to audacity while we suppose we have escaped.
Turns the same warning inside out into a duty, that it concerns us to find our sins out so as to repent of them and forsake them, lest our sins find us out to our confusion and destruction.

themes: if ye will go armed before the LORD to war
then afterward ye shall return and be guiltless
be sure your sin will find you out
do that which hath proceeded out of your mouth
the army of the Lord

schools.summary: Henry sets out the arrangement as a legal instrument, an estate upon condition left to Joshua to declare absolute, and is careful that the penalty was not the loss of all inheritance but the loss of this one, the tribes being compelled to take their lot among their brethren and fare as they fared.

Calvin gives the reason for the conditions, that the two tribes should not afterwards be accused of crossing merely to seek a new home and that deceit should not profit them, and observes that the alternative allotment is not a reward for inertness but a compulsion; Gill notes that the sentence reads as though Moses determined the case himself and supposes it was rather by the vote of the whole court, and takes the singular verb of the reply as a mark of unanimity.

Wesley states the forfeit plainly, that they should lose their possessions in Gilead and be constrained to seek possessions among their brethren; and takes the clause about what the Lord has said either of the present moment or of the older command.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the conditional terms and the repeated promise in their order.

debates.question: Who made the grant?
debates.positions: Gill notes that the text reads as if Moses determined the case himself and supposes it was by the vote and with the consent of the whole court; Calvin agrees that though Eleazar and the elders are not named it is certain they were not passed over, since the case had been brought before them from the beginning, and adds that Moses acted relying on God command even though the text does not say God interposed his authority.

outliers.view: Is precise about what the threatened penalty actually was, not that the two tribes should have no inheritance at all, but that they should not have the one they coveted, and should not expect the lot to favour them.

Reads the confident tone of the arrangement as deliberate encouragement, since in laying down rules for a division of the land as though it were about to happen Moses raises everyone confidence, as if the victory were already in their hands.

themes: Moses commanded Eleazar and Joshua
they shall give them the land of Gilead
possessions among you in the land of Canaan
an estate upon condition
answered as one man

schools.summary: Gill wonders in what form the grant was made, by word of mouth before the court or by an instrument drawn and signed, and notices that the undertaking is repeated again and again for confirmation; Calvin turns the late appearance of half Manasseh into a chronological question and rejects the reading that would put the conquests of Machir after the grant, while conceding he will not contend the point pertinaciously.

Keil and Delitzsch define what was conveyed with the precision of a deed and call it strange that the half tribe should be included here for the first time at the close of negotiations in which it is never mentioned; Ellicott resolves the oddity by pointing forward to the verses showing that a portion of that tribe had conquered parts of Gilead and Bashan and so acquired a just claim.
Henry offers three possibilities for the inclusion and settles on none, adding a reason of his own, that men celebrated for courage were well placed in a frontier country.

debates.question: Why does half Manasseh appear only at the end?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch call it strange, since the half tribe takes no part in the negotiations; Ellicott resolves it from the closing verses, that a portion of the tribe had been chiefly if not exclusively engaged in conquering parts of Gilead and Bashan and had justly acquired a claim to what it had subjugated; Henry offers their own request, divine direction, or their having signalized themselves, chooses none, and adds that it was good policy to put a warlike family in a frontier country; Calvin makes it a matter of chronology, that the portion is excepted because those lands had been separately acquired already.

outliers.view: Argues the chronology from Hebrew narrative habit, that it is common with the Hebrews to transpose the order of occurrences when something omitted is added to explain what follows, and then declines to press the point against anyone who prefers the other reading.

themes: we will pass over armed before the LORD
the kingdom of Sihon and the kingdom of Og
the land with the cities thereof
half the tribe of Manasseh
a claim acquired by conquest

schools.summary: Gill argues the cities were repaired and not founded from the calendar, since these were places long in being and only months remained before the crossing, though he allows that men enough were left behind to be set to work; and he supplies the local traditions, a Talmudic form of one name, the renaming of a city by Herod, and a Targum describing another as the city of two streets paved with marble.

Keil and Delitzsch identify almost every town with a modern ruin and give distances, correct a colleague by name over the site of Aroer, and admit ignorance where a town is mentioned only here; Ellicott argues from probability that new cities would not have been built and the circumstances admitted no such delay, and adds that the Moabite stone was discovered at Dibon in 1868.

Wesley says they had neither need nor leisure to do more, the old cities not having been burnt and ruined as several in Canaan were; Clarke explains the changed names politically, that conquerors called cities after their own names.
Henry gives both reasons for the renaming and adds that the Amorites may have suffered the places to go to decay.

debates.question: Why were the names of the cities changed?
debates.positions: Gill and Wesley give the religious reason, that one name was an idol and another meant the habitation of Baal where a temple probably stood, so that the Reubenites would not retain such titles; Clarke gives a political reason, that conquerors called cities after their own names, instancing the city that took the name of the man who took it; Henry offers both without choosing, either to signify the change of owners or because the old names carried a respect to the deities worshipped there.

outliers.view: Brings the one modern fact into the chapter, that it was at Dibon that the Moabite stone was discovered in 1868.
Notes what undoes the whole renaming, that the text never says what the new names were, and that when the places later fell to the Moabites their ancient names were restored to them.

themes: the children of Gad built Dibon
fenced cities and folds for sheep
their names being changed
repaired and fortified
ancient names restored

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the imperfects as pluperfects on the principle that Semitic narrative sets explanatory clauses before the leading thought, trace Jair descent through a father of Judah who married a daughter of Machir, and reject a proposed identification of Nobah city in favour of the site later geographers assign to Decapolis; Ellicott renders the verse as a pluperfect outright and gives the same descent for Jair.

Calvin reaches the same chronology by argument rather than grammar, that the lands were separately acquired and the portion excepted for that reason; Gill marks the distinction the passage turns on, that the part of Gilead the two tribes asked for was already conquered while the part given to half Manasseh was still in Amorite hands, and reports and rejects the opinion that Machir himself was still alive.

Clarke cites Ainsworth for the observation that the tribes first settled were the first carried captive, names the kings and the places of that captivity, and objects that the name Jair gave his towns ought to have been translated rather than carried over; Wesley makes the same observation his closing remark and calls it a proportion providence frequently observes in balancing prosperity and adversity.

debates.question: Did the conquests of Machir children precede the grant?
debates.positions: Keil and Delitzsch say the imperfects are to be read as pluperfects, the explanatory clauses preceding the leading thought in the Semitic manner, so that the sons of Machir had already taken Gilead when Moses gave it; Ellicott renders it so directly; Calvin reaches the same result by argument, rejecting as unsuitable and improbable the reading that puts the victories after the permission, while conceding that he will not pertinaciously contend against anyone who prefers it.

debates.question: Was Machir himself alive to receive the grant?
debates.positions: Gill reports from Aben Ezra the opinion that he was, and rejects it on the rule that all who came out of Egypt aged twenty and upward died in the wilderness but two; Wesley says the same more shortly, that Machir was doubtless long since dead and the family or posterity is meant.

outliers.view: Explain why Jair line passed into his mother tribe against the ordinary rule, guessing that Machir had portioned his daughter with a rich dowry as though she were an heiress.

Closes the chapter on a symmetry, that as these tribes were placed before the other tribes so they were displaced before them, being carried captive some years earlier, which he takes for a proportion providence frequently observes.

themes: the children of Machir went to Gilead
Moses gave Gilead unto Machir
Jair took the small towns thereof
Nobah took Kenath and called it after his own name
first settled and first carried away
